<meta>This page continues Robert Hooke's technical description of the mechanical components used in his high-precision astronomical instruments. He focuses here on the "Centres and Sockets" that allow for the fine adjustment and measurement of angles.</meta>

The way the **centers** and **sockets** are designed can be seen in Figures 12 and 13. Figure 13 shows them in an end-view **perspective**, while Figure 12 shows a side-view **perspective**. Number 1 is the roller <note>original: "Rowler"; a cylindrical component used to rotate or move parts of the instrument</note> of the upper tube, and 2 is the roller of the lower tube. 3 3 are the screws used to fasten them in the holes. 4 4 is the enclosing or socket-screw that presses tightly against the **cylinder**. 5 and 6 indicate the smooth cylindrical socket that guides the cylindrical screw, ensuring its axis passes exactly over the center of the roller 2 2. By using a **ring (7)** on the screw, the pointed end (8) is held against the support <note>original: "portance"; a bearing or supporting part</note> (9). It is not difficult to understand how to make a dividing plate and its hand or pointer <note>original: "Index"; a pointer on a scientific instrument</note>, nor how it can be turned from the center of the two tubes by a long rod, as shown in *Figure 8*. Once it is determined through observation how many rotations (and what fraction of a rotation) correspond to five whole degrees, it will be easy to calculate a table of *subtenses* <note>original: "Subtenses"; linear measurements used to determine the size of an angle; effectively a table of chords</note>. This table will show exactly what fraction of a turn is needed to measure every minute and second of that angle.

3. In 1665, I achieved the same result using a roller that rolled along the edge <note>original: "limb"; the graduated arc or outer edge of an astronomical instrument</note> of the **quadrant**. This was done with the help of two wires coiled around those rollers, with their ends fastened to the edge of the **quadrant**. By using a large pointer on the end of this roller, I was able to move the arm of the instrument to any five-second interval on the **quadrant** with great ease and certainty.

At the same time, I also built another frame with a straight screw that opened only to five degrees. This used rollers <note>original: "Tumbrels"; here used to describe small cylinders or wheels within the mechanism</note> similar to a pair of dividing *compasses* (using the same method I just described for measuring *diameters* or *distances* up to five degrees). I used very precise <note>original: "curious"; in this period, the word meant highly detailed, expert, or intricately made</note> lines drawn on a smooth glass plate and points very precisely marked at every five degrees on the edge of the **quadrant** (or whatever instrument it was attached to). With the help of a very thick *plano-convex lens* (with its flat side facing down toward the plate and the curved side toward the eye), this frame could be moved five degrees at a time across the entire edge of the **quadrant**. Using this instrument, I could easily and accurately divide an angle into five-second increments.

While the previous section focused on complex seed-syllables, this section begins a systematic dictionary of the primary "Mother" letters (the Sanskrit alphabet), mapping each vowel and consonant to specific deities and cosmic principles.</meta>

# Now Begins the Lexicon of the Mother Letters
### (Mātṛkā-nighaṇṭu)

Having bowed to the Lord of Obstacles <note>original: "Śrī-Gaṇeśa"</note>, the Man-Lion incarnation <note>original: "Nṛsiṃha"</note>, the Goddess of Speech <note>original: "Bhāratī" or Saraswatī</note>, the Supreme Lord <note>original: "Īśvara"</note>, and Shiva, I shall speak this Lexicon of the Mother Letters for the understanding of those with the simple minds of children. || 1 ||

The Fixed One <note>original: "Dhruva"</note>, the Savior <note>original: "Tāra"</note>, the Triple <note>original: "Trivṛd"</note>, the Vast <note>original: "Brahma"</note>, the Beginning of the Vedas, the Immortal Star <note>original: "Tāraka-avyaya"</note>, the Sacred Hum <note>original: "Praṇava"</note>, the Triple-Measured <note>original: "Trimātra"</note>, the Light of the Syllable Om <note>original: "Oṃkāra-jyoti"</note>, and the First One—these are names for the sacred syllable Om. || 2 ||

The Fair-Necked One <note>original: "Śrīkaṇṭha"</note>, He Who Resides in the Hair and Neck, the Path of Return <note>original: "Nivṛtti"</note>, the First of Vowels—the **letter A** <note>original: "A-kāra"</note> is also celebrated as the Mother and the Wind. || 7 ||

The Lord of the Half, the Small Lamp <note>original: "Dīpikā"</note>, the Left Ear, the Slayer of the Demon Madhu <note>original: "Madhusūdana"</note>, Indra, the Primordial One, and the Six-Faced One <note>original: "Ṣaṇmukha"</note>—the **long letter Ū** is known by the name of Protection. || 8 ||

The Radiant One <note>original: "Rocikā"</note>, the Right Nostril, the Immortal Being, He Who Took Three Strides <note>original: "Trivikrama"</note>, the Mother of the Gods, and the Destroyer of Enemies—the **letter Ṛ** is remembered as the Burning Sun. || 9 ||

The Lord of Guests <note>original: "Atithīśa"</note>, the Dwarf Incarnation <note>original: "Vāmana"</note>, the Liberating One <note>original: "Mocikā"</note>, the Left Nostril, the Mother of the Demons, and the Knower of Fate—the **long letter Ṝ** is the Ender of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripurāntaka", a title of Shiva</note>. || 10 ||

<margin>Summons the Skipper and gives him his ship back.</margin>
For he summoned the skipper of the captured ship and asked for forgiveness for the damage sustained, because his intention, when he had them chased, had been to pursue a ship of the Moors from <term>Mecca</term>, as those from <term>Calicut</term> had told him, since he was at war with them. And that it had not been his fault, as they could have prevented all this by saying where they came from and where they were going; but that he wanted to make amends for all this by returning his ship, by acting as a friend to the King everywhere, and by helping him in whatever he might need. The skipper fell at his feet upon this offer, thanked him, received some gifts, and departed from there, well satisfied with his courtesy.

<margin>Complaint to the Samorin about the loading of Pepper.</margin>
The fleet had already been lying here for 3 months and had been held up by the actions of the Moors in the loading, so that every load of pepper came to cost a fourth of a gold <term>pistole</term> <gloss>Spanish or Italian gold coin</gloss>. Pedralvarez was forced, through <term>Correa</term>, to make the Samorin understand that he knew for certain that the Meccans were loading their ships at night. But he received in answer beforehand that if such were true, he would provide for it. Yet Correa and the Admiral, placing little store by these words, decided that at the break of day one would attack the ship of the Moors that one most suspected of loading; and if one found pepper in it, [they would] bring it out of the harbor, carry it into their own ships, and pay the merchants to whom it belonged, notwithstanding the King had said that he wanted to take it from them, because he had forbidden all ships to take that in before they were fully loaded. The Portuguese found themselves deceived in the overpowering of this ship, for instead of pepper, they found it provided with nothing but food, and took the Moors from the ship.

<margin>Plan to raid a ship.</margin>
<margin>Which they do, but are deceived in their opinion.</margin>

<term>Uncia</term> <gloss>ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: 𐆑. It consists of twenty-four <term>scripuli</term>. It is called an <term>uncia</term> because it <term>unciat</term> <gloss>unites</gloss> the totality of the smaller weights into its own unit, that is, it encompasses them. 

<term>Semuntia</term> <gloss>half-ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: S. It is called <term>semuntia</term>, as if half of an <term>uncia</term>. For it consists of twelve <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Duella</term> <gloss>two-thirds of an uncia</gloss>: which is written thus: ƱƱ. It is called <term>duella</term>, as if two <term>sextulae</term>. For it consists of eight <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Sicilicus</term> <gloss>quarter-ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: Ɔ. It consists of six <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Sextula</term> <gloss>sixth of an ounce</gloss>: which is written thus: Ʋ. It is called <term>sextula</term>, as if the sixth of an <term>uncia</term>. For it consists of four <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Dragma</term> <gloss>drachma</gloss>: which is written thus: <note>A cross or X with a horizontal bar through the center</note>. It consists of three <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Emisesela</term> <gloss>half a sextula</gloss>: which is written thus: <note>A lowercase p-shaped character with a cross-stroke through the stem</note>. It is called <term>emisesela</term>, as if half of a <term>sextula</term>. For it consists of two <term>scripuli</term>. 

<term>Scripulum</term> <gloss>scruple</gloss>: which is written thus: ſſ. It consists of eight <term>calculi</term> <gloss>pebbles/smallest units</gloss> or six <term>siliquae</term> <gloss>carob seeds</gloss>. The <term>scripulum</term> is named after a diminution, from a small stone which is called a <term>scrupulus</term>. 

<term>Obolus</term> <gloss>half-scruple</gloss>: which is written thus: —. It consists of four <term>calculi</term> or three <term>siliquae</term>. 

<term>Cerates</term> <gloss>a small weight/carat</gloss>: which is written thus: Z. It consists of two <term>calculi</term>, or a <term>siliqua</term> and a half. 

<term>Calculus</term> <gloss>pebble</gloss>: which is written thus: 𐆑. It is the smallest part of a weight. It is called a <term>calculus</term> because it is as small as a pebble, which is trodden upon without bother. 

If, therefore, you divide anything into twelve parts and take away the twelfth, you will call it an <term>uncia</term>, and the remainder a <term>deunx</term> <gloss>eleven-twelfths</gloss>. If into six, a sixth is a <term>sextans</term>, and you will call the remaining five a <term>dextans</term> <gloss>five-sixths</gloss>. If into four, the fourth part is a <term>quadrans</term>, and the remaining three will be judged by the name of <term>dodrans</term> <gloss>three-quarters</gloss>. If into three, the third is a <term>triens</term>, and you will call the remainder a <term>bes</term> <gloss>two-thirds</gloss>. But if you take five from twelve, you will call the seven remaining a <term>septunx</term> <gloss>seven-twelfths</gloss>; and if five are removed, you will call it a <term>quincunx</term> <gloss>five-twelfths</gloss>. If, however, you divide it into two, both halves are called a <term>semis</term>. The rest can be equally learned and taught by the inspection of the calculation itself, through a certain art of words among those who converse, as much as by the stylus of those who write. But since I have premised something concerning the names and figures of the <term>unciae</term> and fractions, I shall now append how many <term>scripuli</term> accrue to the <term>unciae</term>.

...its construction is truly on the <term>ḍammah</term>, not on a hidden <term>fatḥah</term>. At that time, his words are clearly in line with the first possibility... contrary to the apparent text of the manuscript. If it is so, then it should be interpreted accordingly here and in what preceded. Reflect with fairness.

<insert>His saying</insert> "according to al-Kisāʾī": he only attributed the <term>ḍammah</term> for the <term>Lām</term> to the school of al-Kisāʾī because he expressed it using the term "jussive" <term>jazm</term>, which is one of the titles of declension <term>iʿrāb</term>. No one is followed in that except those who say it is declinable, namely al-Kisāʾī and those who followed him. It is not appropriate to carry his words to a remote school; rather, they should be carried to a school that eases the additions... or it is said that the meaning of his saying "jussive" is to be treated like a jussive. This is supported by the author's previous saying: "the verbs are three." He specifically mentioned the <term>ḍammah</term> for al-Kisāʾī because he is the Imam of the people of Kufa.

<insert>His saying</insert> "to lighten": i.e., to lighten the pronunciation of it. <insert>His saying</insert> "for fear of confusion with the sound-ending present-tense verb in the state of pause." <insert>His saying</insert> "at the need for it": in that the letter after the present-tense prefix is still <term>sākin</term>, as illustrated: the <term>Ḍād</term> in "he strikes" <term>yaḍribu</term> is still, so it is brought [the helper vowel] to reach the pronunciation of the still letter. The letter after the present-tense prefix was not moved... out of fear of two still letters meeting. If that <term>Hamzah</term> [of connection] is not needed, it is not brought, such as when the letter after the present-tense prefix is moving <term>mutaḥarrik</term>, like "he rolls" <term>yudaḥriju</term>...

<column-break/>

The consideration of it being "moving" is by its literal form, not its underlying estimation. Even if it is moving literally but still in estimation—such as "stand" <term>qum</term> and "sell" <term>biʿ</term>—for their origin is "taqūmu" and "tabīʿu"... you say "qum" and "biʿ".

<insert>His saying</insert> "built on stillness": i.e., on the principle in verbs and indeclinability. The principle in verbs is indeclinability, and the principle in indeclinability is stillness <term>sukūn</term>, so one does not ask for their cause. The closest to literal stillness is like "invade" <term>ughzu</term>, and the estimated stillness is like "invade" <term>ughzū</term>, "be angry," and "be strong"... 

If the "Nūn of women" <term>nūn al-niswah</term> is attached, it is built on stillness. If the commentator had said: "The command <term>amr</term> according to Sibawayh is built on what its present-tense is apocopated with, as long as it is not attached to the Nūn of women, otherwise it is built on stillness, or the Nūn of Emphasis, otherwise it is built on the fatḥah like the present-tense in both," it would have been more specific and comprehensive.

<insert>His saying</insert> "and on its deletion at the end if it is a weak-ending verb": i.e., if it is not attached to the <term>Alif</term> of duality, the <term>Wāw</term> of the group, the <term>Yā</term> of the address, the <term>Nūn</term> of women, or a directly attached <term>Nūn</term> of Emphasis. If those are joined to it, then in things... as he ruled by his saying: "or on its deletion and the Nūn." But he did not mention the ruling of the <term>Nūn</term> of women and the <term>Nūn</term> of Emphasis, which is known from what preceded: that with the first it is built on stillness, like "strike ye [fem.]," "invade ye," "fear ye," and "throw ye"; and with the second it is built on the <term>fatḥah</term>, like "invade [thou] indeed," "fear indeed," and "throw indeed."

<insert>His saying</insert> "The four extras": "extras" <term>zawāʾid</term> is the plural of "extra" <term>zāʾidah</term>...

(Third reason): Because it remains in its own nature. For example, a terrestrial substance remains terrestrial in all conditions and does not change into something else. Similarly, understand that substances of water, fire, air, and ether also do not deviate from their own nature. 3. (Fourth reason): Because it is perceived by the five senses. The substance is perceived by the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose. Tastes and qualities cannot be perceived by all five senses. 4. (Fifth reason): Because the substance is the support. The substance is independent, whereas tastes, qualities, potencies, and post-digestive transformations all rely upon the substance. 5.

"Because of the capacity for action." Actions are rooted in the substance. For instance, collecting Vidārīgandhā, pounding it, and cooking it—all these actions are rooted in the substance, not in the tastes. 6. "Because of the authority of the scriptures." In the scriptures, the substance is considered primary. In the instructions for formulas, such as for the citron (<term>mātuluṅga</term>) and the <term>agnimantha</term>, the substances are taught, not just the tastes. 7.

"Because the tastes depend on the sequence of the substance." Tastes depend on the condition of the substance. For example, in a young substance, the tastes are young; in a mature one, they are mature. 8. "Because diseases can be cured by a part of the substance." Diseases can be cured even by a portion of the substance, such as the latex of the <term>mahāvṛkṣa</term> <gloss>spurge tree</gloss>. Thus, the substance is primary. 9.

The definition of a substance is that which possesses action and qualities and is the inherent cause. 10.

# Pelliot chinois 3113

Regarding the equipment for luxury robes and the rules for **not losing the privilege of the robe** <note>During the Kaṭhina period, monks are permitted to be separated from their three robes without committing an offense. "Losing the robe" refers to the expiration of this special privilege.</note>. In the midst of water, if a few people draw water, even at night; or as some say, within the constant flow of a river, one must not stop or bury [the boundary]. 

The markers for the boundary are determined by eight trees, seven intervals, and sixty-two steps. These serve to partition the surface. If we discuss the **Pavāraṇā sheds** <note>Pavāraṇā (self-correction) is the ceremony held at the end of the rainy season retreat; "sheds" refers to the temporary structures or designated areas for this rite.</note>, there are fifteen types:

1.  Where the Sangha is absent, and the two times are not listed.
2.  Fruit trees, where the trees are interconnected; it is permitted for someone to guard them, and the interior is restricted by a screen.
3.  Where gaps are established by ten fingers' width <note>A traditional unit of measurement in the Vinaya.</note>, specifically screened; if in a place with fruit, it must be treated four times over.
4.  Where the establishment is constant.
5.  Where the middle is not yet reached.
6.  Where practitioners walk a great distance and return; the interior is double-screened. 
7.  If the area is insufficient, six types of boundaries are listed; the boundary is for the time of return and the location.
8.  A wooden boundary; "middle" refers to the markers of the fields where one stays.
9.  A screened boundary; after the screening, the time is fixed to the location.
10. A room boundary; a place where many scattered repairs are made.
11. A house boundary; where numbers are stored in six locations.
12. **An island boundary**; involving lakes or rivers; if one studies there, even if the time passes, one does not lose the robe privilege.
13. **A well boundary**; involving secret paths and irrigation; if one stays overnight and places their robe there, they do not lose the privilege during their stay.
14. [Missing in original sequence]
15. A boundary where there are many people, or a small sea, or the sands and stones of the south. <gloss>Bulrushes</gloss> A path through the surging waves. These two boundaries are established by name.

There are two types of "reaches" <note>likely referring to coastal or river reaches</note> at the boundary's edge. When people of three types arrive, seeking a common residence, they establish the **Kaushambi** <note>original: 憍薩彌 (Qiāosàmí). This likely refers to a legal precedent or specific tradition regarding the Kaṭhina robe from the city of Kosambi.</note> foundation. If there are people within the boundary together with the monastery, or if they are outside the boundary, or if they are not in order, the boundary may be large or slightly different. If they merge into one later, it follows the Kaushambi extension.

If within a large boundary there is a monastery, and the outside of the boundary is not confused and does not flow together, then later scriptures mention villages like Tangmai and Yicun. 

According to the **Vinaya** <term>Vinaya: The code of monastic discipline.</term>, if there is no established Law <note>Dharma-rule</note>, and one is within a village, the robe is protected. Because this matter is not yet according to the Law, the "Path" is considered the Law. It does not matter if there is a village or not; the Law of the Vinaya flows through. If a village existed first, one follows the Law and later establishes the unified "Golden Cloister." 

If an outsider has not yet entered, the rule states that the head of the teaching is not within the boundary. If one departs from the village, a new boundary path is made. If there is a village marker, and the village acts improperly, it is called an "Empty Kaṭhina." According to the meaning, one seeks the Kaṭhina through the village marker. If it is not a Kaṭhina, the robes are not yet relinquished. 

If a person enters and the robe is not under the Kaṭhina boundary, and they stay within the riverbed, the robes accumulate merit to the limits of the village. If the village is gone, or if the markers of the teaching are not established, it is not a robe boundary. This is fixed. Therefore, next we remove the robes and the deep Kaṭhina teachings. This is the ultimate discussion.

**Question:** When there is a village, can one borrow it first? How is the Kaṭhina removed?
**Answer:** According to the Vinaya, it does not matter if it exists or not. One first observes the surroundings, then relinquishes the robe. If the relinquishing of the robe follows the Law, one can first establish the Kaṭhina markers. If one speaks of the method of removal, and says it follows the previous village markers, the current Law is not the Kaṭhina. 

Regarding the **Taking of the Kaṭhina**: The Vinaya says if a village existed previously, first observe the surroundings and rely on the previous clothing. If one takes the Kaṭhina outside the boundary, that is the "True Kaṭhina." Because it is a new Law, it is called the "Path Kaṭhina Boundary." If it is doubled, it is a new name and does not depend on the boundary. Among those who follow the Law, the witnesses manage the matter. In harmony, they follow the Law to modify and fix the robes. If the various parts of the body are too short or mismatched, it is decided by the Law.

Between the Kaṭhina and the village boundaries: one follows the markers of the village. The village boundary is the Kaṭhina boundary. Furthermore, when many people divide the merit, they obtain the boundary. Regarding the village, if one enters the village against the flow: 
According to the Vinaya, at the very beginning, there is a gap of one Kaṭhina. The "Faithful Kaṭhina" robe follows the Law. Furthermore, if one acts as a boundary companion, and the place fully has the Kaṭhina, the boundary is within the path. 

**Question:** Regarding staying overnight with the Kaṭhina robe? 
**Answer:** One follows the Law. If there is a gap, one follows the Law. Whether it is Kaṭhina or not, if it is by a river or stream, and the boundary is scattered or the boundaries of the "Color Limit" are fallen, and people do not know the markers: if there are houses in the middle, the robe rule says one must know the method of steps. Whether it is Kaṭhina or not is determined by the "Kaṭhina of Faith." One follows the twelve steps and relies on the gap. If this single gap of the robe is not a village, the markers are few. One can name it the "Kaṭhina of Faith." If the houses are not mismatched, they share the same nature.

There are three types of "Staff Paths": 
1. Utilizing the robe boundary and releasing many.
4. The village path in two places, with Kaṭhina markers appearing to be exhausted.

One checks the numbers and followers, then later determines the **Natural Kaṭhina of Faith**. Those who are not following the Law refuse the boundary and the restricted path of the Kaṭhina. Using the name of the path to differentiate a single interval, the Kaṭhina boundary does not follow the Law. Because of this, within the Kaṭhina boundary, there is a Natural Kaṭhina boundary. 

The signs do not necessarily need to be six or seven. For instance, in a village, most are village boundaries. If they are fixed and established and do not rely on each other, or if they are divided according to the Law, then the markers are for the Buddha's Law. The Kaṭhina signs rely on themselves. Afterwards, one marker, once it receives the Kaṭhina, if it rises to refuse the Law, it is the Kaṭhina marker. 

Within the curves, one follows the "Bucket Kaṭhina Boundary" and trusts it. Secondly, following the Law, one trusts the Kaṭhina boundary. Because of this boundary Law, within the two, a natural faith arises. The power of the two boundaries is divided; each boundary naturally has a Kaṭhina robe boundary. Because the exterior place does not follow the Law's modification, there is power.

If it is not according to the Law, it is the "Correct Kaṭhina." This "Surging Shape" below creates the Kaṭhina robe markers. Below it creates the Law Kaṭhina, which is also a flowing robe. The judgment of the flow is exhausted by the teaching robe's minimal division. Facing the "Correct Kaṭhina," the Vinaya calls it the "Fixed Kaṭhina." Following the Law provides the strength of the Kaṭhina robe. 

The **Natural Kaṭhina Robe** has "Bridge Stones" upon which the strength is divided. There is an explanation of the markers, as there were errors previously. 
**Question:** Regarding the strength of the Natural Kaṭhina land? 
**Answer:** The robe can be separated like a breast-child <note>Meaning it can be legally separated from the monk's person</note>. If one seeks the division of strength, it is the restricted Law outside the village markers. If that village is not a village, the land outside the markers where the strength is divided is where the "Heart-Governing Stone" is located. The **Kaṭhina Stone Boundary** is a type of stone boundary. 

1. A Natural Kaṭhina that does not disappear. The Vinaya recites that one side has a "Face-Washing Marker." Half of the text says the "Initial Hair Screen." This is also it.
2. Kaṭhina Ponds, etc. Looking at the Kaṭhina's construction, they are shown together. The Kaṭhina exists only within the Kaṭhina; it is not outside. It is also named "Not-Nine."

C.P. to Nepos, Greetings.
You ask that I take care to review and amend my little books, which you have so eagerly acquired. I shall do it; for what should I more willingly undertake, especially when you request it? For since a man most grave, most learned, most eloquent, and—above all—most occupied, who is about to be a provincial governor, thinks it of such importance to carry our writings about with him, I must take care that this part of his baggage does not offend you as if it were superfluous. I will strive, therefore, first that you may have these companions as convenient as possible; and second, that when you return, you may find others that you would wish to add to them. For you, as my reader, do not encourage me to new works in a mediocre way. Farewell.

C.P. to Falco, Greetings.
It is the third day since I heard Sentius Augurinus with my greatest pleasure, or rather, admiration. He calls them poems. Many things were handled delicately, many sublimely, many with charm, many very tenderly, many sweetly, many with bite. I think that for some years, nothing of this same genre has been written more gravely or perfectly, unless perhaps his love for me deceives me, or the fact that he carried me himself to the heights with his praises. For he took for his theme the subject that I sometimes play with in verse. And afterward the one prostrating shall arise and bow upward until all the prostrate have bowed. And afterward all the pious of the group shall lament, and all of them fall one upon the back of the other until all the prostrate of the great one have bowed. And afterward they shall return to their place in great weeping and great wailing upward. And thus all of them every day and every Sabbath and every month upon the sanctuary and the festival of peace, in great weeping and wailing to the Holy One, blessed be He, and He shall have mercy upon them, [granting] the redemption of their soul speedily, amen. And all those things written by the hand of Daniel, all of them shall be fulfilled. And they shall pray and weep before the Creator of the world and shall say, "May it be Thy will before Thee that Thou have mercy upon us and redeem us from this bitter exile by the merit of our holy fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, peace be upon them, and the merit of Moses and Aaron and David and Solomon, and the merit of all the righteous and the pious and the innocent and the good deeds that were in this world." And they shall be there for three days in that day, and this rectification they perform always and every Sabbath and festival. And every person shall say in great weeping and great wailing and shall say, "When shall we merit to see the building of the Holy Temple speedily in our days, amen."
